Convergent truncations bounded strictly between1 and2
Find a stable value and bound the error

question: If \(x\) equals \[ \sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+\sqrt{1+\cdots}}}}, \] then:
solution:
Interpret the infinite radical through its finite truncations. Let
\[
u_1=1,\qquad u_{n+1}=\sqrt{1+u_n};
\]
then \(u_n\) is the expression with \(n\) square roots. We will find a number that these truncations approach.

A nonnegative number unchanged by adding another outer square root satisfies
\[
r=\sqrt{1+r},\qquad r^2-r-1=0.
\]
The quadratic formula gives \(r=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2\). The negative root cannot equal a principal square root. Let
\[
\phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
It satisfies \(\phi^2=1+\phi\), and hence \(\phi=\sqrt{1+\phi}\). Also, \(1<\sqrt5<3\) gives \(1<\phi<2\).

Starting from \(1=u_1<\phi\), the recursion preserves the bounds \(1\le u_n<\phi\): if they hold for \(u_n\), then
\[
1\le\sqrt{1+u_n}<\sqrt{1+\phi}=\phi.
\]
To prove that the truncations actually approach \(\phi\), rationalize their difference:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\phi-u_{n+1}
&=\frac{\phi^2-u_{n+1}^2}{\phi+u_{n+1}}\\
&=\frac{\phi-u_n}{\phi+u_{n+1}}\\
&\le\frac{\phi-u_n}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The denominator is greater than \(2\), so it is nonzero. Repeating this bound gives
\[
0\le\phi-u_n\le\frac{\phi-1}{2^{n-1}}.
\]
Successive halvings make this upper bound smaller than any prescribed positive error. Thus the finite radicals approach \(\phi\), establishing the value of the infinite expression. Therefore
\[
x=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad 1<x<2,
\]
which is choice C.
